entities.summary:
Amanieu d'Albret (died 1520), a scion of the powerful House of Albret, was a French Roman Catholic cardinal whose career unfolded against the tumultuous backdrop of the Italian Wars and the politically charged Borgia papacy. Born into a prominent Gascon noble family with extensive landholdings and influence in southwestern France, his elevation to the cardinalate in 1500 by Pope Alexander VI cemented the Albret family's ecclesiastical power and their strategic importance in the intricate web of Franco-papal relations. His life exemplified the deep intertwining of aristocratic lineage, church office, and secular power characteristic of late medieval and early modern European elites.

Following his nomination by King Louis XII of France, Amanieu was created Cardinal-Deacon of San Nicola in Carcere. His cardinalate was marked by active participation in the Curia, where he served as an influential voice for French interests. He held numerous ecclesiastical benefices, including the bishoprics of Oloron (1499-1520) and Condom (1500-1520), and later the archbishopric of Bordeaux (1520), consolidating significant wealth and authority within the French church. Beyond his ecclesiastical duties, Amanieu d'Albret was deeply involved in the political and military machinations of the era, notably accompanying Cesare Borgia on campaigns in the Romagna and participating in diplomatic missions that sought to navigate the shifting alliances between France, Spain, and the Papal States.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Amanieu d'Albret's career as a cardinal and diplomat significantly advanced the political and ecclesiastical interests of the powerful House of Albret and French influence in the Papal States during the tumultuous Italian Wars. His life exemplifies the deep entanglement of secular power and church office in early modern Europe, contributing to the broader context of pre-Reformation challenges.
